short: The OECD AI Principles are a Recommendation of the OECD Council adopted in May 2019 and revised in May 2024. They set five values-based principles for trustworthy AI and five recommendations to governments. They are not law, and they supply the definition of an AI system that the EU AI Act and several national laws copied.
title: OECD AI Principles
subtitle: The 2019 intergovernmental standard on trustworthy AI, revised in 2024, adopted by 47 jurisdictions
body_html:
What the OECD AI Principles are

The OECD AI Principles are the Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, adopted by the OECD on May 22, 2019. They were the first intergovernmental standard on AI. The G20 endorsed a version a month later. The Recommendation was revised in May 2024, after the OECD updated its definition of an AI system in November 2023 to cover generative models and systems that act with varying autonomy.

A Recommendation is soft law: adherents commit to it politically, not legally. There are 47 adherents: the 38 OECD members, the European Union, and eight non-members, Argentina, Brazil, Egypt, Malta, Peru, Romania, Singapore and Ukraine.

What it covers

Five values-based principles for all actors:

  • Inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being
  • Human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy
  • Transparency and explainability
  • Robustness, security and safety
  • Accountability

Five recommendations to governments: invest in AI research and development, foster an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem, shape an enabling policy environment, build human capacity and prepare for labor market transition, and cooperate internationally.

Why it matters

The principles are the common ancestor of the AI laws written since. The EU AI Act's definition of an AI system was aligned to the OECD's 2023 definition during the final negotiation so that the two would match. The NIST AI RMF cites the principles. The G7 Hiroshima process was run with OECD support. When a company says its AI policy follows international principles, these are usually the principles.

What a claim does not mean

Adherence binds governments, not companies, and binds them politically. A company cannot be certified against the principles and a country cannot be sanctioned under them. The OECD AI Policy Observatory tracks national implementation; that tracking is the only enforcement.

Related instruments

The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI covers similar values with a larger membership. The G7 Hiroshima Code of Conduct applies them to advanced AI developers. The Council of Europe Framework Convention is the binding treaty version. See the Standards and Frameworks hub.

Primary sources

  • Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449, full text and adherents
